_about: Plain-English 'What does this mean?' notes for the 30 Find-your-match (v2) statements. Shown only on request while answering. Written without party names, leaders, slogans or branded policy names so the voter answers on the principle, not on who is associated with it. Figures are rounded context from official statistics (Stats NZ, Treasury, Ministry of Justice, Ministry for the Environment) as at October 2026; they describe the situation, not a position.

explainers.E1: Income inequality is usually measured by comparing the highest-earning households with the lowest. Reducing the gap can be done through higher taxes on high incomes, bigger transfers like benefits and tax credits, or higher minimum pay. The trade-off is that some people keep less of what they earn so that others receive more. Agree if you think narrowing the gap is worth that; disagree if you think people should keep more of their own income even if the gap stays wide.
explainers.E2: Governments can lower taxes, which leaves people with more money to spend as they choose, or keep taxes up and fund more public services (health, schools, transport, welfare). You cannot have the maximum of both. Agree if you think people spending their own money does more good; disagree if you think pooled spending on services does more good.
explainers.E3: Income from a job is taxed as it is earned. Gains made when a house, shares or a business rise in value are, with some exceptions, not taxed in New Zealand. Taxing those gains like wages would raise revenue and treat different kinds of income the same, but would also reduce returns for people who own assets, including retirement savings and family homes if they were included. Agree if you think all income should be treated alike; disagree if you think gains on assets should be treated differently from wages.
explainers.E4: Some services can be run by government-owned organisations or by private companies competing for customers. Supporters of competition argue it lowers prices and improves service; supporters of public ownership argue essential services should be run for the public rather than for profit and that competition does not always work for things like power lines or housing. Agree if you generally trust competing businesses to deliver these better; disagree if you generally trust public ownership.
explainers.E5: Benefit obligations are conditions such as looking for work, attending appointments or enrolling children in school. Sanctions reduce or stop payments when conditions are not met. Firmer rules aim to move more people into work; the cost is that some households, including children, have less money when a sanction is applied. Agree if you think firm obligations are right even with that cost; disagree if you think payments should not be cut in that way.
explainers.E6: Pay can be negotiated person by person, workplace by workplace, or across a whole industry (for example all cleaners or all bus drivers) with unions negotiating on behalf of everyone doing that job. Industry-wide bargaining tends to lift pay and conditions at the bottom, and tends to raise costs for employers and reduce flexibility. Agree if you think industry-wide bargaining is the better protection; disagree if you prefer pay set at the workplace or individually.
explainers.E7: Government borrowing pays for spending now and is repaid, with interest, from future taxes. Keeping debt low leaves room to respond to future shocks and keeps interest costs down; spending more now on health and education may improve services sooner but adds to debt. New Zealand's government debt is moderate by international standards and has risen since 2020. Agree if you think holding debt down should come first right now; disagree if you think health and education spending should come first.
explainers.S1: Longer sentences keep people who have committed serious crimes in prison for more of their lives. Supporters say this protects the public and reflects the harm done; critics point to the cost (tens of thousands of dollars per prisoner per year), prison overcrowding, and evidence that longer sentences do little to reduce reoffending. Agree if you think longer sentences are worth those costs; disagree if you think the money and effort are better spent elsewhere.
explainers.S2: Police powers to stop, search or move people on are limited by law to protect civil liberties, and expanding them has in the past affected some communities more than others. Wider powers may deter crime and disorder and make public places feel safer; they also mean more people who have done nothing wrong are stopped. Agree if you think safer public places justify wider powers; disagree if you think current limits should stay.
explainers.S3: This is about how far the state should go in regulating choices adults make about their own bodies and lives, with drug use as the example. One view is that adults should decide for themselves and that criminal penalties cause more harm than the behaviour; another is that the law should discourage harmful choices to protect people and communities. Agree if you lean toward personal freedom here; disagree if you lean toward the law discouraging such choices.
explainers.S4: Public institutions such as schools decide how to handle matters like gender identity, sexuality and different family structures in what they teach and how they operate. One view is that they should reflect changing attitudes and include everyone; another is that these are matters for families and that institutions should not move ahead of what parents and communities want. Agree if you think institutions should reflect changing attitudes even over objections; disagree if you think they should defer to parents and communities.
explainers.S5: Free expression is protected in New Zealand law, with limits for things like incitement and defamation. The question is where to draw the line between protecting speech and protecting people from harm, including online. Agree if you think speech should be protected even when it offends or is felt to be harmful; disagree if you think stronger limits are justified to prevent harm.
explainers.S6: Young people who offend can be dealt with mainly through the youth justice system and support services (family group conferences, education, housing and welfare help) or through firmer consequences such as military-style programmes, detention or being treated more like adults. Agree if you think tougher consequences are the right response; disagree if you think support and services should remain the main response.
explainers.T1: Te Tiriti o Waitangi is the 1840 agreement between Māori and the Crown. Many laws and public agencies now refer to it, and some services are designed or delivered differently for Māori as a result. One view is that this is the right way to honour the Treaty and close gaps in outcomes; another is that laws and services should be the same for everyone. Agree if you think the Treaty should keep shaping laws and services this way; disagree if you think it should not.
explainers.T2: New Zealand has a separate Māori electoral roll with its own seats in Parliament, and some councils have Māori wards; some public services are designed specifically for Māori. One view is that everyone should be treated identically regardless of ancestry; another is that these arrangements reflect the Treaty and are needed to give Māori a fair say and to close gaps in outcomes. Agree if you favour identical treatment with no specific arrangements; disagree if you think such arrangements should remain.
explainers.T3: Shared decision-making (sometimes called co-governance) means Māori groups and the Crown or councils decide together about resources such as rivers, forests or coastlines, often through settlement arrangements. Supporters say this reflects the Treaty partnership and brings better long-term care of resources; critics say it slows decisions and gives one group a say others do not have. Agree if you support shared decision-making over natural resources; disagree if you think elected bodies alone should decide.
explainers.T4: The Treaty's meaning in law has largely been worked out case by case by the courts and the Waitangi Tribunal, which interprets the Treaty principles. Another approach is for Parliament to define what the Treaty means in legislation. Agree if you think elected MPs should settle the legal meaning; disagree if you think it should continue to be interpreted by the courts and the Tribunal.
explainers.T5: Te reo Māori is an official language and tikanga (Māori customs and protocols) are increasingly used in public settings, such as bilingual place names, agency names and school programmes. Agree if you think this should grow even though some people object; disagree if you think it has gone far enough or should be scaled back.
explainers.T6: Treaty settlements are negotiated agreements that acknowledge and compensate for historical breaches of the Treaty by the Crown, typically with an apology, money and the return of some land. Most large groups have settled or are in negotiation; some claims remain. Agree if you think the process should be wound up now; disagree if you think it should continue until remaining claims are resolved.
explainers.V1: Protecting the environment (water quality, native species, emissions) often means limits on farming, building, mining or driving that reduce economic output or raise costs. Agree if you would accept slower economic growth for stronger protection; disagree if you think growth should not be sacrificed.
explainers.V2: New Zealand puts a price on most greenhouse gas emissions through the Emissions Trading Scheme, but agricultural emissions, about half the national total, are not priced. Pricing them would give farmers a reason to cut emissions and would raise the cost of some food; pricing industry more would raise fuel and energy prices. Agree if you think emitters should pay even if prices rise; disagree if you think the cost to households and farms is too high.
explainers.V3: Large projects need consents under environmental law, which can take years. Faster approval processes reduce delay and cost for things like roads, mines, wind farms and housing, but reduce the checks and public input that protect the environment and local communities. Agree if you think faster approvals are worth fewer checks; disagree if you think the checks should stay as they are.
explainers.V4: New Zealand has pledged under the Paris Agreement to cut emissions by set amounts by 2030 and to reach net zero by 2050. Meeting the pledges costs money, including possibly buying overseas carbon credits, while some larger countries are doing less. Agree if you think New Zealand should keep its word regardless; disagree if you think it should scale back if others do less.
explainers.V5: New Zealand has coal, gold, oil and gas, and other minerals on land and offshore. Extracting more would bring royalties, jobs and export income that could fund public services; it also carries environmental risks and adds to emissions. Agree if you think more extraction is a good way to pay for services; disagree if you do not.
explainers.O1: Migration adds workers, skills and demand to the economy and also adds pressure on housing and infrastructure. Lower migration can ease that pressure and lift wages in some jobs but leave some businesses short of staff. Agree if you think New Zealand should admit fewer migrants even with staff shortages; disagree if you think current or higher levels are right.
explainers.O2: Most new residents can access some benefits and public support after two years; some supports have longer waits. A longer wait reduces costs to taxpayers and asks newcomers to contribute first; it also leaves some migrant families without a safety net if things go wrong. Agree if you think several years is a fair wait; disagree if you think newcomers should have access sooner.
explainers.O3: New Zealand is a close partner of Australia, the United States and the United Kingdom but has kept some distance, for example its nuclear-free policy, and is not a member of every alliance arrangement. Closer alignment might bring more protection and influence; independence keeps more freedom of action and avoids being drawn into others' conflicts. Agree if you prefer an independent foreign policy; disagree if you favour closer alignment with traditional allies.
explainers.D1: New Zealand is a representative democracy: Parliament makes most decisions, with occasional referendums. Binding referendums let voters decide big questions directly but take time and money, and can reduce a complex issue to yes or no. Agree if you want more major decisions put to a binding public vote; disagree if you think Parliament should decide.
explainers.D2: Political parties can currently receive donations from individuals, companies, unions and other organisations, with disclosure rules above certain amounts. Limiting donations to enrolled voters would cut organisations' influence and reduce the money available to campaign. Agree if you think only individual voters should be able to donate; disagree if you think other donors should still be allowed.
explainers.D3: Councils make decisions about local services, planning and rates, but central government can set rules they must follow or override them. More local freedom means decisions fit local wishes but can differ from place to place; more central control brings consistency. Agree if you prefer local councils deciding; disagree if you prefer central government setting the rules.
